text: Zadra gives the order, his people go down into the sewers, and the film goes with them. Warsaw, the last days of the uprising, a unit already reduced to a handful: the fighting above has narrowed to a single practical question, which is where to come up. Andrzej Wajda made Kanał in 1957, close enough to the events that the choice of setting works as an argument and not a device. Underground, rank thins out. Ninety-six minutes spent mostly below street level, tracking how long a shared purpose lasts in conditions that make seeing impossible and talking dangerous. The tunnels are dark and they branch, and a group that stays together moves at the speed of whoever is slowest, which is the whole of the film's suspense.

A death in an interrogation room is, before it is anything else, a problem of paperwork: a body to account for, a form to sign, a version of events that has to hold. What follows widens outward, from the room to the men who need the file closed, then to people with no official reason to care. Korea in 1987, under a military government, and 129 minutes built like a thriller because everything turns on who learns what, and when. Jang Joon-hwan splits the telling among many hands rather than one hero, so no single act of nerve looks decisive by itself and none of them is optional either. Critics writing on Korean films of this kind keep returning to how the decade should be remembered. This one answers structurally: nobody in it is placed to fix anything alone.

Sixty-two minutes, nearly all of them in a room where a young woman answers questions from men who have already settled what her answers mean. Rouen, 1431, the Hundred Years' War still running: French soldiers of a rival faction took her, a church court tries her, and her English enemies oversee the room. Robert Bresson stays inside the procedure, question and answer and the next question, so the film becomes a matter of language under load, one exact sentence set against a system built to hear it wrongly. Everything outside that room stays outside it. The Maid of Orléans is a defendant here, seated, and the drama is entirely in what a person will and will not say when saying it costs. Short films about long trials are rare, because the compression is expensive; this one spends the savings on attention.

The dress costs more than the household has, and Bob has decided that his daughter will wear it to her First Communion regardless. Everything after that is arithmetic: what can be sold, borrowed, carried, or done for cash, and who will have to be asked. Ken Loach shoots it in the register of ordinary weeks in Britain in 1993, where work comes and goes and the parish calendar does not move. The comedy is real; so is the arithmetic; they are not kept in separate scenes. Ninety minutes driven from end to end by a purchase that a wealthier film would treat as a detail, and the engine is a father's refusal to let the day be smaller than the one he pictured. That refusal is stubbornness. It is also the nearest thing to a principle he can currently afford.

The thriller machinery here is largely paperwork: statements taken, tapes labelled, questions put in rooms where the door has been closed on purpose. Northern Ireland during the Troubles, and an American lawyer, Ingrid Jessner, is on the ground to document what the state has been doing to people there. The case she ends up carrying needs Peter Kerrigan, a British investigator prepared to work against the government that employs him. Ken Loach keeps the rhythm of an inquiry rather than a chase, so what advances the story is a document changing hands, or a witness deciding in the space of a pause whether to speak. The place supplies the intimidation without help. Everyone here knows the rules; the open question is which of them will behave as though the rules were real.

On an island off the coast, thirty-one men with criminal records are trained to kill the leader of North Korea, and then the mission is called off. The unit came out of January 1968, after commandos crossed the other way with orders concerning President Park Chung-hee; the answer was assembled quickly and then left in place. That interval afterwards is the film's real subject. Soldiers held at pitch for an operation that no longer exists, on a rock they cannot leave, with nobody able to say what the waiting is for. Kang Woo-suk works at commercial scale, 135 minutes of drills and weather and rising temper, and pressure inside a closed place travels sideways, toward whoever is nearest. It is drawn loosely from something that happened, which changes how the drills look.

A man is sent south to kill a dissident, and what he does instead is take up with a South Korean agent who has a grievance of his own. Jang Hoon builds on proximity rather than pursuit: two men with incompatible employers, doing work together that neither can report. The premise commits the film to long stretches of watching and being watched at close range, shared hours and shared tasks, each keeping a version of himself the other is not meant to see. That is where the tension lives, more than in any exchange of fire. A hundred and seventeen minutes, and the arithmetic that matters is trust between two people trained to withhold it, in a city where both are officially someone else. Loyalty here is not a feeling. It is a bill that keeps coming due.

The classroom is a slab of painted board strapped to a man's back, and it moves at walking pace. Kurdish teachers cross the hills near the Iraqi border during the Iran-Iraq war, looking for anyone who will stop long enough to be taught, and almost nobody stops. Said joins a group of old men trying to reach a village that has been bombed and offers to guide them; Reeboir attaches himself to boys hauling contraband across the border, who keep moving because soldiers patrol the roads. Samira Makhmalbaf holds the film to 85 minutes and keeps it on foot, so lessons arrive in fragments, mid-journey, between other business, a marriage among it, to Halaleh, the clan's only woman, a widow with a young son. The board is a tool, a burden, and a claim about what these men are for.

A painter who drinks all day and works all day is an awkward subject for a film, since neither activity has much plot in it. Im Kwon-taek takes the awkwardness as the job. Jang Seung-eop, remembered as Chihwaseon, is met already fluent, so the drama comes from what surrounds the fluency: drink, company, the small things he keeps finding worth a second look, and Mae-hyang, through whom the question of fate reaches him. Two hours in which the decisive events are strokes of ink on paper. That requires making brushwork legible as action, holding on hands and surfaces well past the point where a historical drama would ordinarily cut away. The argument, made mostly by looking, is that a life can be organised entirely around a skill and still not be accounted for by it.

The offer is plain: produce a suspect the public will accept for a run of murders, and the promotion follows. The murders are background in Ryoo Seung-wan's film, not subject. What the camera stays with is the negotiation, and with a detective who has been honest partly because nobody had yet made dishonesty worth the trouble. Once he agrees, the case stops being an investigation and becomes construction work: a story assembled to fit a man, rather than a man located to fit the evidence. A hundred and nineteen minutes, quick on its feet, with the pleasures of a procedural bolted onto something nearer to office politics conducted with warrants. The damage is not counted in bodies. It is counted in how many times a thing has to be agreed to, out loud, in an ordinary tone of voice.

The canvas is transparent and the camera sits on the far side of it, so the marks arrive from nowhere, in order, with no hand attached. Picasso paints, Henri-Georges Clouzot records, and that apparatus carries all 78 minutes. Early pieces resolve in a stroke or two. Later ones accumulate, get buried, get contradicted: a figure painted over, a colour that takes the composition somewhere else, a version that exists briefly and then does not. Watching a work being revised is nothing like watching one finished. The film keeps producing images that are good and then losing them on purpose, which makes a peculiar kind of suspense out of whether what is on the surface now will survive the next decision. What it records is not talent so much as choosing, over and over, at speed.

An old woman in bed waits for news of her son, and her daughter-in-law brings it, and invents it. János is in prison on a charge the family understands to be political and does not name aloud. Luca comes, sits, supplies what is wanted, and goes back to a life the older woman knows nothing about. Hungary, 1971, 88 minutes, much of it at a bedside, where Károly Makk works with two women and a fiction that has to be renewed at every visit. The care and the lying are the same action, performed by the same hands, and the film will not separate them. There is no villain in the room. What comes from outside the door arrives inside it as tenderness, which is a strange thing to watch and a hard thing to leave.

Old Oliva tells the town's children about his years at sea, about Diana, and about a cat that wore sunglasses. While he talks, a strange circus is arriving. Vojtěch Jasný made this in Czechoslovakia in 1963 and gave it the shape of a children's story told at adult length: 104 minutes of comedy in which the impossible element is introduced calmly and then allowed to stay. A small town is a useful instrument for a device like that, since everyone in it holds a position worth protecting, and an unexplained animal makes positions visible. The frame matters as much as the fable: everything here reaches an audience through an old man's telling, and a tall tale told to children is a licence to test the adults.

In the 1970s the divers of Kunchon went down without equipment and came up with whatever could be sold, and then that trade thinned out. Smuggling replaced it, and the fit was exact: goods dropped into the water need people willing to go under and retrieve them, and Choon-ja and Jin-sook have done that work all their lives. Ryoo Seung-wan builds his action on the fact, which puts a good deal of the film below the surface, where nobody can speak and everything is timed against air. On land, the business grows past what a village that size can absorb, and that is the other plot, the one with more edges. 129 minutes of period crime that keeps count of wages, of who is owed, and of what a friendship is worth once money sits on both sides of it.
